performers: Clifford Curzon, piano; National Symphony Orchestra; Enrique Jordá
intro: Clifford Curzon and Enrique Jordá play all three of Falla’s “symphonic impressions” on a six-side Decca set made in London in 1945. The first opens with a harp played close to its soundboard, and the piano is silent for the whole first page.

sections.label: C · En los jardines de la Sierra de Córdoba

cues.title: Harp near the soundboard
cues.text: Allegretto tranquillo e misterioso, in 6/8. The harp plays sulla tavola, close to the soundboard; violas play sul ponticello; cellos and basses pluck. The piano, the soloist, says nothing yet.
cues.evidence: Falla, Noches en los jardines de España (Max Eschig, 1923, full score M.E. 687), I, printed page 3: Allegretto tranquillo e misterioso, dotted crotchet = 50, 6/8; harp “sulla tavola”; violas “sul ponticello”; pizzicato cellos and basses; piano resting. https://archive.org/details/nuitsdanslesjard00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano enters
cues.text: Just over a minute in, the piano enters with a fast, ringing figure marked “ben marcato”, over long wind and horn notes that die away (“perdendosi”).
cues.evidence: Eschig 1923 full score, I, printed page 5, from rehearsal figure 3: piano “ben marc.”, flutes, clarinets, horns and trumpets “perdendosi”. https://archive.org/details/nuitsdanslesjard00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First swell
cues.text: At “Poco più animato” (dotted crotchet = 66) the first full-orchestra swell arrives: winds and harp enter together and the piano pours out broken chords.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1923 full score, I, printed page 8, rehearsal figure 5: “Poco più animato”, dotted crotchet = 66, with winds, harp and piano written out together. https://archive.org/details/nuitsdanslesjard00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Begun in Paris
cues.text: Falla began the piece in Paris in 1909. It was first played at the Teatro Real in Madrid on 9 April 1916, with José Cubiles as soloist and Enrique Fernández Arbós conducting; Falla played it himself in Granada that June.
cues.evidence: Archivo Manuel de Falla, chronology: 1909, “Begins to compose Noches en los jardines de España”; 1916, 9 April at the Teatro Real (Cubiles, Arbós) and 26 June at the Palace of Charles V, Granada (Falla at the piano). https://www.manueldefalla.com/en/paris-1907-1914 https://www.manueldefalla.com/en/madrid-1914-1919

cues.title: In Falla’s own words
cues.text: Falla’s note says the three “symphonic impressions” aim only to “evoke places, sensations, and sentiments”, and that “melancholy and mystery have their part also.”
cues.evidence: Falla’s own note on the work, quoted in Jessica Schilling’s programme note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/2450/nights-in-the-gardens-of-spain

cues.title: A long rise and fall
cues.text: Here the movement builds across a minute or more to its biggest sound, the whole orchestra in full cry, then thins until it is almost silent before the second movement.
cues.evidence: The build, the climax and the near-silence that follows can all be heard in this recording. Columbia’s 1954 Spanish catalogue lists the movement’s closing part, “En el Generalife. Conclusión”, on a record side of its own. https://www.eresbil.eus/web/uploads/archivosGeneradorWeb/Catalogos/erelib_NL0212CAT_01_v.pdf

cues.title: Danza lejana
cues.text: Allegretto giusto, in 3/4. Four solo violas play a trill with mutes over pizzicato cellos and a solo double bass; flutes and cor anglais answer, pianissimo and marcato.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1923 full score, II, printed page 35: Allegretto giusto, crotchet = 100; violas (4 soli) “con sord.” trilling, cellos (4 soli) and double bass (1 solo) pizzicato; flutes and cor anglais “pp marc.” at rehearsal figure 1. https://archive.org/details/nuitsdanslesjard00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The piano at Granada
cues.text: On 26 June 1916 Falla played the piano part himself at the Palace of Charles V in Granada, with the Madrid orchestra under Arturo Saco de Valle. Diaghilev and Massine were in the audience.
cues.evidence: Archivo Manuel de Falla, chronology for 1916, and its page “The Ballets Russes and Spain”. https://www.manueldefalla.com/en/madrid-1914-1919 https://www.manueldefalla.com/en/the-ballets-russes-and-spain

cues.title: Attacca subito
cues.text: Danza lejana ends on repeated piano chords growing louder, flutes and oboes rising in the last bar, and the score says “Attacca subito”. The third movement follows at once, Vivo, with cymbals, a piano chord and trills across the strings.
cues.evidence: Eschig 1923 full score, printed page 56: piano chords “cresc.”, winds “ff”, strings rising, “Attacca subito”; printed page 57: III, En los jardines de la Sierra de Córdoba, Vivo, dotted crotchet = 132, cymbals “ff vibrato”, piano chord, string trills. https://archive.org/details/nuitsdanslesjard00fall
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Piano phrases over hazy strings
cues.text: After the opening storm, a calmer stretch brings what the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s note calls “crystalline, guitar-inspired” phrases for the piano over hazy strings; the drama returns soon after.
cues.evidence: Jessica Schilling’s programme note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic describes the third movement’s orchestral storm, then “a remarkably crystalline, guitar-inspired series of phrases … set for piano over hazy strings”, then the return of the drama. The calmer stretch is audible in this recording. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/2450/nights-in-the-gardens-of-spain

cues.title: The final five minutes
cues.text: The piece “roars through its final five minutes”, in the Los Angeles Philharmonic’s words, with harsh full-orchestra interruptions. On this three-disc set the closing portion, “En las sierras de Córdoba. Final”, fills the last side.
cues.evidence: Schilling’s note for the Los Angeles Philharmonic (final five minutes). Columbia’s 1954 Spanish catalogue lists RG 16053 as “Danza lejana. Conclusión” and “En las sierras de Córdoba. Parte 1”, with “En las sierras de Córdoba. Final” on the last side. https://www.laphil.com/musicdb/pieces/2450/nights-in-the-gardens-of-spain https://www.eresbil.eus/web/uploads/archivosGeneradorWeb/Catalogos/erelib_NL0212CAT_01_v.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A ballet that never was
cues.text: Diaghilev first wanted to make a ballet of Nights. Falla was not keen, and the contract the two men signed was for The Three-Cornered Hat instead.
cues.evidence: Roger Nichols, booklet note for Garrick Ohlsson’s Falla recital (Hyperion CDA68177): Diaghilev “was interested in the idea of making a ballet out of Nights”, but the composer was not keen; they signed a contract for El sombrero de tres picos. https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA68177

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Clifford Curzon (piano), National Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Enrique Jordá (conductor)
fields.note: The Spanish catalogue calls the orchestra the Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional de Londres. Individual players are not identified.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Complete work for piano and orchestra, three movements, on six 78-rpm sides
fields.note: The Internet Archive item lists the three movements and the Spanish catalogue lists the parts on each side. The orchestral edition and any cuts are unknown.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Stated in the discographical note of the Internet Archive item. The sources consulted give no second statement of the date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: Stated in the Internet Archive item’s discographical note. A 2021 review places the later LP remake of July 1951 in the same hall.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Three 78-rpm discs supplied in an album.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Decca X 10020–22 (British issue); RG 16051–16053 (Spanish catalogue numbers)
fields.note: The Internet Archive item gives X 10020–22; the Spanish catalogue of 1954 gives RG 16051–16053 for the same performers and work.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Six sides, matrices AR 9689-2, 9690-2, 9691-1, 9692-1, 9693-2, 9694-2; the Spanish catalogue divides the work as Generalife parts 1 and 2, Generalife conclusion, Danza lejana part 1, Danza lejana conclusion with Sierra de Córdoba part 1, and Sierra de Córdoba final
fields.note: Matrix numbers and side divisions come from two independent listings. Which matrix belongs to which side is not stated.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: The item is in the Internet Archive’s satyr78rpm collection; no personal mastering credit is given.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The item was uploaded on 11 July 2022; the date of the transfer itself is not stated.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: Equipment, equalisation and restoration settings are not stated. The file is one continuous MP3 of the six sides.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Falla died on 14 November 1946. Spanish law protects the works of authors who died before 7 December 1987 for life plus 80 years, so his music remains protected in Spain until the end of 2026; arrangements and modern editions carry their own rights
fields.note: A phonogram term assessment does not clear the composition, an arrangement or a modern score edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU phonogram public-domain basis: published no later than 1954, before 1963
fields.note: The set is listed in Columbia’s Spanish catalogue of discs published up to 1 January 1954, and a 2021 review says Decca remade the work on LP in July 1951 because the 78 set had been so fine, which places the set before 1951. Its actual first issue date is not established here. This is a territorial phonogram basis, not US or worldwide clearance and not a Creative Commons licence.

facts: Piano with José Tragó in Madrid (first prize, 1899); composition with Felipe Pedrell from 1901
Guided by Paul Dukas and Debussy; friends with Albéniz, Ravel and Ricardo Viñes
Gregorio Martínez Sierra and María Lejárraga · Diaghilev and Massine · Picasso · Lorca

quote.text: For everything that concerns my trade, my homeland is Paris.
quote.source: Falla to Ignacio Zuloaga, Granada, 12 February 1923; Archivo Manuel de Falla

composer.background:
As a boy in Cádiz, Manuel de Falla governed a city of his own. Colón had a council, newspapers and a theatre, and according to Roland-Manuel’s 1930 biography the triumph of the day there was El conde de Villamediana, an opera seria composed and conducted by a certain Manuel de Falla. He kept the city running for six years. The real boy was born on 23 November 1876 at 3 Plaza de Mina and meant to be a writer. At seventeen, he told Roland-Manuel in 1928, a conviction at once timid and deep sent him towards composition.

In Madrid he studied the piano with José Tragó and won the conservatoire’s first prize in 1899. Two years later he asked the Catalan musicologist Felipe Pedrell to teach him; from Pedrell, he told his biographer Jaime Pahissa, came the clearest and most solid guidance for his work.
